Parrish is one of the few modern masters. His technical craft was without peer. Unfortunately he is not as highly regarded as he should be since much of his career was as a commercial artist. That, coupled with the fact that he actually enjoyed a lucrative career, keep art snobs from recognizing what a talent he really was. He had an extremely LONG career--starting in around the 1890s and painting up until the early 1960s (basing this on my often faulty memory). He pretty much abandoned painting figures (i.e. people) in the late 1930s and focused primarily on landscapes thereafter. His work is photo-realistic, but not in a gimmicky way--his technique involved layering colors methodically to achieve a hyper-realistic appearance. He is highly regarded for his ability to paint trees and fabrics (amongst other things). Parrish is truly one of the greatest American artists of all time. I HIGHLY recommend folks read more about him and check out his work from the multiple eras in his career.

"in chemistry stability has a very specific definition. It is determined by the free energy of the product compared with the reactant of a reaction. This is a thermodynamic property. Now taking a look at two allotopes of carbon (an allotrope is different structural form of the same element): graphite and diamond, we see that by converting diamond into graphite, the free energy is -2.9 KJ/mol.
